title: The Lesson I Learned From Jeremiah’s Doubts
paragraphs:
The Lesson I Learned From Jeremiah’s Doubts
When God Calls You, But Fear Tells You You're Not Enough
There are moments in life when God places something on your heart so deeply that you cannot escape it.
A calling.
A conviction.
A burden.
A purpose.
Yet instead of moving forward, you hesitate.
You look at your limitations.
Your failures.
Your past.
Your weakness.
And suddenly the voice of fear becomes louder than the voice of God.
I know that feeling because I learned it through one of the most relatable men in Scripture—a prophet whose story begins not with confidence, but with doubt.
Jeremiah.
The man chosen by God before he was even born.
Yet the first thing we hear from him is not courage.
It is fear.
Not certainty.
But insecurity.
Not strength.
But hesitation.
And if we are honest, that sounds a lot like us.
The story begins in Jeremiah 1:4-5:

"Now the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee, and I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations."
The Hebrew word translated "knew" is יָדַע (yada), a deeply personal word that means far more than intellectual awareness. It speaks of intimate relationship, personal recognition, and covenant love.
Before Jeremiah ever knew God, God knew Jeremiah.
Before Jeremiah had accomplishments, God knew him.
Before Jeremiah made mistakes, God knew him.
Before Jeremiah struggled with fear, God knew him.
And still called him.
Let that sink in.
God did not choose Jeremiah because of his qualifications.
God chose Jeremiah despite everything Jeremiah believed was wrong with him.
Yet Jeremiah's immediate response reveals a struggle many believers know all too well.
Jeremiah 1:6:
"Ah, Lord GOD! behold, I cannot speak: for I am a child."
The Hebrew expression begins with אֲהָהּ אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה (ahah Adonai YHWH), a cry of distress that could be understood as:
"Oh no, Lord God..."
Jeremiah wasn't celebrating.
He was panicking.
He wasn't excited.
He was overwhelmed.
God had just revealed a divine purpose.
Jeremiah immediately responded with reasons it could not happen.
"I cannot."
Two words that have buried countless dreams, ministries, callings, and acts of obedience.
I cannot lead.
I cannot serve.
I cannot forgive.
I cannot change.
I cannot speak.
I cannot be used.
I cannot overcome.
Yet Jeremiah's story reveals something life-changing.
God never asked Jeremiah to be enough.
God simply asked Jeremiah to trust the One who is.
God's response is one of the most powerful answers to human insecurity found anywhere in Scripture.
Jeremiah 1:7-8:
"But the LORD said unto me, Say not, I am a child: for thou shalt go to all that I shall send thee... Be not afraid of their faces: for I am with thee to deliver thee."
Notice what God did not say.
He did not tell Jeremiah to believe in himself.
He did not tell Jeremiah to increase his self-esteem.
He did not tell Jeremiah to discover his inner power.
Instead, God redirected Jeremiah's attention away from himself and back to God.
Because the solution to fear is not greater confidence in ourselves.
It is greater confidence in Christ.
Many of us spend years waiting to feel ready.
But Scripture repeatedly shows that God uses people who feel unready.
Moses doubted.
Gideon doubted.
Jonah resisted.
Peter failed.
Thomas questioned.
Jeremiah feared.
Yet God rewrote every one of their stories.
Because grace has always been stronger than weakness.
This is where Jeremiah's story becomes deeply personal.
Many believers quietly carry the fear that their flaws disqualify them.
Some carry shame from past sins.
Others carry wounds from childhood.
Some carry regret.
Others carry secret battles nobody knows about.
Many sit in church wondering if God could ever truly use someone like them.
Jeremiah reminds us that God has never been searching for perfect people.
He has always been transforming broken people.
The Apostle Paul would later echo this same truth in Greek when he wrote:
Ἀρκεῖ σοι ἡ χάρις μου (Arkei soi hē charis mou)
"My grace is sufficient for thee."
(2 Corinthians 12:9)
The word χάρις (charis) means grace, favor, kindness freely given.
Not earned.
Not deserved.
Not purchased.
Given.
That single word summarizes the entire Gospel.
Because the Gospel is not a story about strong people finding God.
It is a story about God rescuing weak people through Jesus Christ.
And nowhere is that seen more clearly than at the cross.
Jesus did not die for the qualified.
He died for sinners.
For doubters.
For failures.
For people who thought they were beyond redemption.
For people like Jeremiah.
For people like us.
The scandal of the Gospel is that God knew everything about us and still chose to love us.
Every hidden sin.
Every secret thought.
Every failure.
Every compromise.
Every moment of rebellion.
Yet Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
That is why our theme remains as true today as it was thousands of years ago:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He rewrites shame into testimony.
Fear into courage.
Failure into redemption.
Brokenness into beauty.
Sinners into saints.
The enemy wants you focused on your limitations.
Jesus wants you focused on His sufficiency.
Jeremiah learned that lesson.
Eventually, the fearful young man became one of history's boldest prophets.
Not because he stopped being human.
But because he learned that God's faithfulness was greater than his doubts.
Maybe today you feel like Jeremiah.
Maybe God is calling you to trust Him deeper.
Maybe He is asking you to step forward in obedience.
Maybe fear has convinced you that you are too broken, too weak, too old, too young, too sinful, or too unqualified.
But Jeremiah's story stands as evidence that God specializes in rewriting impossible stories.
The same God who knew Jeremiah before birth knows every detail about you.
The same God who called Jeremiah still calls people today.
The same God who sustained Jeremiah through hardship still sustains His children now.
And the same Jesus who died and rose again is still transforming lives through grace.
If this message spoke to your heart, don't keep it to yourself.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else needs today.
God's calling is bigger than your doubts.
Because somewhere tonight, another Jeremiah is doubting.
And somewhere tonight, God is still calling.
The voice that called him is the same voice calling you.
And grace is still writing stories nobody thought could be redeemed.
